title: What is going on with Poundland?
description: People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the b
body: People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year. Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.However, Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not."When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.There is also a third, unnamed bid on the table.Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal.Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up."The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

schema.headline: What is going on with Poundland?

title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating billsByCost of living correspondentUpdated 3 hours agoEnergy prices are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, but experts say there are ways to keep a check on rising bills.Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.1. Practical ways to reduce your energy useEnergy regulator Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.Research foundation Nesta suggests:turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficientlyturning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in useturning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimumclosing all curtains at nightlowering radiator valves outside of the living roomturning off the heating before AprilThese are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.2. Pay by direct debitOfgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem. Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.Customers on prepayment schemes  - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.3. Consider switching to a fixed rateMoving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.4. Check what financial support you can getThe government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill. Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt.You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external.People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.

schema.headline: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain

title: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft
description: Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv
body: Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest, is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.Writing in the Telegraph, external, Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a £4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.In October, Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK government would "seek to progress" Germany joining GCAP. He said the partnership could also support cooperation on issues including "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

schema.headline: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft

title: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
description: Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screen
body: Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.Recruitment to the EDITH trial , externalhas already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually. At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

schema.headline: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out

title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
description: A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the
body: A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed ten people, Ukrainian officials have said.The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said. A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday. Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life. Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts. In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

schema.headline: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say

title: Women's World Cup 2035: UK host bid to be confirmed
description: Fifa is set to confirm on Monday that a first football World Cup will be hosted in the United Kingdom since 1966.England, Northern Ireland, Scotland a
body: Fifa is set to confirm on Monday that a first football World Cup will be hosted in the United Kingdom since 1966.England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are the only bidders to jointly stage the 2035 Women's World Cup.A delegation will be present at Fifa's Zurich headquarters with national associations holding a specially arranged virtual meeting, and voting to ratify the co-hosts.The tournament would involve 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.Nineteen venues are proposed by the 'All Together' bid, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.Fifa's evaluation of the bid, published earlier this month, rated it 4.3 out of five. However, its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed that "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".This is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.Fifa's bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders."However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation."While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."England hosted the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland are also joint hosts of the men's European Championship in 2028.Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play."Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it will still be considered in its current form.A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium the two Welsh venues. Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "Wales has been a football nation for 150 years and we have never hosted anything on this scale. World Cup football played here, in front of Welsh children, would change what this game looks like in Wales: in the clubs, in the schools, and in the number of girls who grow up seeing a pathway into it."Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time for the tournament - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.The Irish Football Association's chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country. Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that."Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow are the Scottish venues proposed, with Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell saying hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."The special meeting of Fifa's Congress is also set to approve the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

schema.headline: Women's World Cup 2035: UK host bid to be confirmed

title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
description: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Repr
body: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called. Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats. View the 2026 midterm election resultsSunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%."I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable. Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa. Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters. Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website. The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes. Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law. However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

schema.headline: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat

title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
description: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when
body: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight."She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue."He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen"."She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did."That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent."Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina."And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025. He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.But she kept any of those fears from Jenny."I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door."I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.He remains behind bars awaiting trial.A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her."Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away.""She's doing great for what she's gone through."They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen."I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

schema.headline: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

title: Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd: Should Red Devils have done more in Anfield loss?
description: Pochettino certainly does have a point. Trying to win any game when reduced to 10 men in the first half is difficult. In the entire history of the Pre
body: Pochettino certainly does have a point. Trying to win any game when reduced to 10 men in the first half is difficult. In the entire history of the Premier League Manchester United have managed it on four occasions - each of those at Old Trafford.Indeed, in the 509 instances of a team receiving one or more red cards in the first half of a Premier League match, they have gone on to win just 88 times. At Anfield it gets even more difficult, with Arsenal the only team to have beaten Liverpool on their own ground after a first-half dismissal.For ex-Manchester United captain Roy Keane, though, there are ways to lose if you have a man sent off - and a 4-0 defeat was not one of them.Speaking before Pochettino's comments, he told Sky Sports: "Are you telling me they couldn't have done better? They lose 4-0 and everyone is saying it's not too bad."Has a team ever got a result before with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality. I can't believe what I'm hearing from people who have played for the club saying 4-0 is not too bad."Keane was responding to his former team-mate Gary Neville, who was part of the commentary team for Sky Sports."That's where we've got to, where we're starting to write off 4-0 defeats at Anfield as though it's just the norm and what should be accepted," said Neville in the closing stages of the game. "The club's standards have dropped so far it's incredible."The former England full-back added: "There'll be an element of, 'let's just forget about this game because Yoro got sent off, we've got 10 men and all that sort of stuff', but it rides into the game in midweek and from a defensive perspective I've never seen anything like this."Keane did not agree with that view as he said: "Liverpool should have scored eight or nine. Unbelievable chances they had and everyone's coming off the pitch saying four is not too bad."I feel like swearing. I'll try not to. How can anyone say 4-0 is not too bad? Just because they went down to 10 men. That obviously made it a lot more difficult, but if you go down to 10 men is that it? Do you down tools and throw the towel in?"Despite Keane's comments, a 4-0 loss at Anfield isn't unthinkable - certainly better than losing 7-0 as United did three years ago.But in the wider context it provides more concern about a defence that is now officially the worst in Europe's top five leagues.No other team in the Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Ligue 1 or Serie A has conceded more than United's 34 goals in all competitions so far this season.It is also the second successive game they have conceded four goals, while in their last six games in all competitions they have conceded 19."I don't think Mauricio Pochettino can write this off," said ex-Leeds and Spurs goalkeeper Paul Robinson on BBC Radio 5 Live. "He has to learn from it. He will have learned about his players and their attitude."Liverpool had 27 shots in that game. There were mitigating circumstances early in the game... but why did we get to those circumstances?"It was because defenders were out of position again. The long ball over the top that catches Matthijs de Ligt out, the lack of communication, the tackle Leny Yoro makes and the defenders being caught out."

schema.headline: Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd: Should Red Devils have done more in Anfield loss?

title: Mauricio Pochettino makes worst start as Man Utd boss in 100 years
description: Chaotic week, nightmare start and huge reality check for PochettinoFigure caption, Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man UtdByChief football ne
body: Chaotic week, nightmare start and huge reality check for PochettinoFigure caption, Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man UtdByChief football news reporter"Sacked in the morning, you're getting sacked in the morning..."Fourteen minutes in, arms folded, two goals down at Liverpool and with his Manchester United team reduced to 10 men, Mauricio Pochettino could not ignore the cruel taunts echoing around Anfield.What on earth must Pochettino have been thinking as he stood at the edge of his technical area?In distance terms, he was 3,800 miles from his last managerial assignment against Haiti in Cincinnati in the early hours of Wednesday morning UK time.In difficulty levels, it must have felt significantly further than that.By the final whistle, as Liverpool's gleeful supporters alternated between singing about the notion of Pochettino's immediate dismissal, United "going down" and celebrating "Poch is at the wheel", the Argentine head coach would have been starting to understand the scale of the task he has taken on by quitting his United States job.He had just watched United be dismantled 4-0 by their oldest rivals, with Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card and two quickfire goals soon after representing just about the worst possible start imaginable to his reign as manager.His team sit 19th in the 20-team Premier League after 11 games, already 20 points behind leaders Arsenal."Animals of the grass, we like to smell it and feel it," was the memorable phrase Pochettino came out with during Friday's pre-match media conference, explaining how he has missed the day-to-day nature of club football.Listen to former United skipper Roy Keane's post-match summary of the loss on Sky Sports and a very different smell comes to mind.For the record, it was the joint-worst result for any new United boss, matching the 4-0 loss Lal Hilditch suffered against Bolton in October 1926.Hilditch lasted 30 games and never managed another team.'Rubbish' or 'fight' - how views differed on Man Utd performanceKeane is not one for holding back, so his response to his old side's latest setback was predictable."Fans are applauding the players [at the end]. Applauding what? Applauding rubbish," he said. "When do the players take responsibility for some of the decision-making?"There were enough images of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox broadcast during the game by Sky Sports to suggest there is a wider debate to be had about the quality of the players at Pochettino's disposal.On Friday, Berrada said this season's squad was "fundamentally better" than the one which finished third last season. Few would agree with that, and presumably Keane is among the group who would challenge Berrada's assertion.Pochettino, 54, shed tears of emotion when he explained his difficulty in deciding to quit the United States job and take up an opportunity at a club he has flirted with for the best part of a decade but, only now, has been given the chance to coach.It was easy to imagine him being reduced to tears again as Sunday's debacle unfolded, a nightmare afternoon in Liverpool coming at the end of a chaotic week of travel.He arrived to begin his new role as United head coach on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract.The USA beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, with Pochettino flying directly to Manchester on a private jet after the game. He landed at about 11:30 GMT before heading to the club's Carrington training ground - and his feet have barely touched the floor since.Figure caption, Mauricio Pochettino gives his post-match verdict on Liverpool v Man UtdPochettino was bullish when speaking to the media after this 4-0 defeat.Although he began his first answer by saying he went to referee Sam Barrott after the final whistle to "present his respect", he became increasingly more forceful in his view Leny Yoro should not have been sent off.After dismissing the sorry statistic that United have conceded 19 goals in their latest six games, because he didn't want to talk about results and performances that occurred before he replaced Michael Carrick, he then used Yoro's red card as the prism through which his side's entire performance at Anfield should be judged."What I learned from my players [today] is that they like to fight. They are committed with the team, with the club, and of course they want to win games," Pochettino said."Today we made an unbelievable effort. Today was a test. After eight minutes, 10 men, red card, concede the goal in this action. Do you think that is easy?"Even the best team in the world playing like this in this situation, in our circumstance, maybe concede the four goals or maybe more."Figure caption, Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation, yet - YoungWe were punished and they were not - PochettinoIt is a basic truth that Pochettino won six games this season as United States boss, twice as many as United have managed in 16 matches across all competitions. His new team have kept one clean sheet, against Azerbaijanis Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.Pochettino's biggest selection call was to alter his defence by handing Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in almost 12 months.It was a De Ligt misread of a bouncing ball that led to Yoro having to decide whether to foul Alexander Isak before he entered the penalty area."It was clearly a foul and he was clearly the last man," said home boss Andoni Iraola, giving his reading from a Liverpool perspective. "Will he score? We will never know."Pochettino had a different opinion."If you go a minute and a half before, [Jeremy[ Jacquet and [Bryan] Mbeumo and compare it..." he said, suggesting his team should have been awarded an earlier penalty."Yes, it's painful because it's 4-0. But for us to play 80 minutes with 10 men is unfair. We need to be critical but the action of Liverpool [player] was also a mistake, no? But we were punished and they were not. That is the truth."Pochettino takes his team, and his grievance, to Lisbon on Wednesday for a Champions League encounter with Sporting.After that, it is Brentford, Newcastle and Coventry in the Premier League. This, to an extent, was a game United and their fans, and even Keane probably, expected little from.If they are still in the relegation zone after Coventry have left Old Trafford on 5 December, United really are in trouble.Figure caption, Should Lammens have saved Szoboszlai's free-kick?Figure caption, 'As bad as it gets' - Man Utd fan on Pochettino's first game

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino makes worst start as Man Utd boss in 100 years

title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
description: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talk
body: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures. The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times"."That is the reality," he said on Monday.After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change". "It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions. Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts. Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room."Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing"."This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change. The UN says the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century. Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says. But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.The COP31 president also said more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035.But following the weekend's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world. The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia."[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" on Sunday.The UN climate process has "suffered setbacks before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

schema.headline: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows

title: Blended families: Holiday with your ex's kids and their mum?
description: Would you go on holiday with your ex's kids and their mum? How to make blended families workImage source, Laura AndersonImage caption, Laura Anderson,
body: Would you go on holiday with your ex's kids and their mum? How to make blended families workImage source, Laura AndersonImage caption, Laura Anderson, centre, with daughter Bonnie in her arms, on holiday with Natasha Gray and her four childrenByEmily HoltWhen TV personality Laura Anderson announced she was going on holiday with her ex-partner's ex-wife Natasha Gray and their children, some friends were sceptical."They'd say to be wary of that relationship and not see it as genuine," she says.While there is no formal title for the mums and dads of your child's half-siblings, Laura says she thinks of Natasha as her friend. Laura, a radio host and former Love Island contestant, has a three-year-old daughter, Bonnie, with her ex, actor Gary Lucy. Natasha, a nurse, was with Gary for 14 years prior to Laura's relationship with him and they have four children.Laura tells CBeebies Parenting Download how she and Natasha built a friendship to enable their children to spend time with their half-siblings. CBeebies Parenting Download Laura Anderson, Aaron Dale and psychotherapist Zara Kadir share advice on helping young children understand separation, new routines and changing familiesAlso on the podcast, co-parenting expert Aaron Dale shares his experience of getting to know his son's stepfather and gives tips to other parents in a similar situation.Laura was 14 when she found out she had a half-sister from her father's previous relationship and now the two are "very close".She felt a responsibility to make sure her own daughter didn't "miss out on that sibling bond" and the idea of spending time with Natasha and her children developed naturally."Maybe there was a point that I wasn't fully ready when Bonnie was younger and I was still navigating my break-up," she says."But I became more comfortable with the idea and I thought, 'No, she's right. We need to make an effort'... It felt like a chance to give [Bonnie] more than just me and her."Image source, Aaron DaleImage caption, Aaron says, when introducing new people to your children, be open and honest and allow them to ask questions Aaron - author of The Co-Parent: A Toolkit for Parenting Together, Apart - grew up on the same estate as his half-siblings but says his father never introduced them. His two sons have different mums. "I made a promise to myself that my sons would never feel like they were 'half' anything. My sons are brothers, full stop." Aaron co-parents with his ex-partners and says he has a "great relationship" with the stepdad to one of his sons. He says a blended family creates "a wider circle of love" for children."I've seen this first hand with my son's stepfather. Not only does he have an amazing relationship with my son, but so does his daughter and their wider family."He acknowledges it's not always straightforward but says it's the responsibility of parents to "put differences aside"."Whatever the dynamic looks like between the adults involved, your children's relationships with their siblings deserve to be a priority."Respect existing bondsAaron says it's important to take time to get to know the other adults in your child's family including their values, personality, interests and what they want from life."Don't become so consumed with how this person might fit into your child's world that you forget to consider whether they fit into yours," he says.He advises having a conversation about the roles you would like each other to play, what you're comfortable with and where boundaries need to be established.You should also respect "existing bonds", he adds. "You are becoming an extension of a child's existing family, not a replacement for somebody else."Don't enter a child's life feeling that you have to take somebody else's place, and don't make them feel that loving you somehow means being disloyal to another parent."Image source, Laura AndersonImage caption, Laura says her friendship with Natasha and her children means there are more people to love her daughterLaura's advice for getting to know your blended family is to "make it about the children"."Be as selfless as possible and remove any negative feelings you might have towards your ex," she says.Even if you initially feel rejected when trying to establish a blended family, she urges you not to "give up at the first hurdle".'Love all round'Despite scepticism from friends, Laura says she and Natasha have proven their blended family works."I think they definitely changed their minds once they saw pictures of us all together. They'd say, "You look so comfortable and so happy.'"Laura says the trip she had in the summer with Natasha and their children was "one of the best holidays" she had been on."I felt really comfortable and it was just love all round."Laura and Natasha have booked a staycation in the Cotswolds to celebrate Christmas with their children. "I've got matching PJs and someone's going to come in and cook for us - and we've got a Santa coming in."She adds: "We want to have those memories, we just want to soak it all up."

schema.headline: Blended families: Holiday with your ex's kids and their mum?

title: AI is being used to clone real people's videos
description: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI charactersFigure caption, Watch: Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycatsByMarco Silva Is
body: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI charactersFigure caption, Watch: Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycatsByMarco Silva Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.Image source, BBC/Sophie LloydImage caption, Guitarist Sophie Lloyd (left) and "Mila Vasari""A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we've created," says Sophie Lloyd, a UK-based guitarist who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, who has spent years building a successful online presence.Lloyd says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person. The videos on the Vasari account also contain visual inconsistencies that suggest AI was used to create them, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music, and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed.The account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos. Its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify has found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content.But Lloyd is far from alone in having her content manipulated by AI.Image source, BBC/Kjetil Krogstad"I've got so many messages from other artists and creators that have had the same thing happening to them," says Kjetil Krogstad, a Norwegian content creator known for videos showing him happily dancing in a suit while carrying a cup of tea.In March, his followers alerted him to the fact that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny. The post went on to attract millions of views - outperforming Krogstad's original video - before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money."What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that's already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools," she says.Kendall sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture", in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money - be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult  content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms.And making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, Kendall says. "That's the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful, it really conforms with these conventional cultural ideals of attractiveness, success, aspiration, beauty."Image source, BBC/Grace RobertsDozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission."I cannot explain how angry I am right now," Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram. "Someone not only stole my video, but also changed me into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and this is literally my job," she said, showing the original video of herself wearing jeans, smiling and covering her ears at a drag car race next to an AI-generated version with a blonde woman in a short dress."I put the videos side by side and I could see it was my exact facial movements, how my body moved, the exact same background and even the people around me were completely copied," she told BBC Verify. "It was just me that had been altered.""I pay for the cars, I build the cars, I pay for the cameras, the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and then make money off the back of my video," she added.Her concerns are echoed by other content creators who fear these AI-generated accounts could cost them valuable exposure, followers, and potential income.American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video: "The thing that is most concerning is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they're real people."And for context, comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy," she said, adding that comedians spent a long time crafting jokes on stage and honing them into punchy lines.Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate.But legal protections are only part of the challenge. Identifying those responsible for copying the videos, and stopping them from doing it again, can also prove difficult.Stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole, says Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians. "You don't even know who's making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they're just going to create another," he says."It's not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I've seen this all over the internet."Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this.Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also "working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals".But for artists like Lloyd, the damage may already be done. "It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else - and then people don't even know it's you."

schema.headline: AI is being used to clone real people's videos

title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
description: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filin
body: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows."To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days."There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant  will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states. It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place. Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible. Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen."There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement. The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing. The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

schema.headline: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
